471.title: Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale – Baseline
471.description:
Safety Interventions Instructions for HEP

As a safety precaution, all participants who endorse suicidal ideation on the C-SSRS must be referred for psychiatric evaluation. Please plan ahead for this possibility by creating a list of local mental health providers to be given to participants if needed.

- Participants who score a 4 or 5 in the ‘Current’ column of page 2 of the C-SSRS (active suicidal ideation with or without a plan) must be referred for immediate evaluation in your site’s emergency department or by on-site psychiatric staff.

- Participants who score a 2 or 3 in the ‘Current’ column of page 2 of the C-SSRS (passive suicidal ideation) must be referred to a mental health provider for psychiatric evaluation within 1 week, using the aforementioned list of providers.

If you have any questions or concerns as to the severity of a participant’s suicidal ideation, please contact Dr. Andres Kanner at 847-476-1811 (or if Dr. Kanner is unavailable, Dr. Siddhartha Nadkarni at 917-763-1016) to determine the necessity for acute intervention.

With all psychiatric referrals, the phenotyping clinician should explain to the participant that the interview suggests that they should seek evaluation by a mental health provider; please emphasize that this is not a clinical diagnosis. For adolescents (under age 18), the participant’s parent or guardian must also be notified immediately of any suicidal ideation, including if the parent/guardian is not present during the C-SSRS administration. Lastly, with all referrals, please also ask for written permission from the participant and/or parent or guardian (if under age 18) to contact their primary care provider and notify them of the participant’s C-SSRS score indicative of suicidal ideation.

After completion of the study visit:
- fill out the HEP Safety Intervention Form, and
- follow up with the participant 1 week after referral to confirm they were able to schedule an appointment with a mental health provider.

1.12.field_title: 3. Active Suicidal Ideation with Any Methods (Not Plan) without Intent to Act
1.12.field_description:
Subject endorses thoughts of suicide and has thought of at least one method during the assessment period. This is different than a specific plan with time, place or method details worked out (e.g. thought of method to kill self but not a specific plan). Includes
person who would say, “I thought about taking an overdose but I never made a specific plan as to when, where or how I would actually do it…..and I would never go through with it.”

1.13.field_title: Lifetime: Have you been thinking about how you might do this?

1.36.field_description:
A potentially self-injurious act committed with at least some wish to die, as a result of act. Behavior was in part thought of as method to kill oneself. Intent does not have to be 100%. If there is any intent/desire to die associated with the act, then it can be considered an actual suicide attempt. There does not have to be any injury or harm, just the potential for injury or harm. If person pulls trigger while gun is in mouth but gun is broken so no injury results, this is considered an attempt.
Inferring Intent: Even if an individual denies intent/wish to die, it may be inferred clinically from the behavior or circumstances. For example, a highly lethal act that is clearly not an accident so no other intent but suicide can be inferred (e.g., gunshot to head, jumping from window of a high floor/story). Also, if someone denies intent to die, but they thought that what they did could be lethal, intent may be inferred.

1.60.field_description:
When the person is interrupted (by an outside circumstance) from starting the potentially self-injurious act (if not for that, actual attempt would have occurred).
Overdose: Person has pills in hand but is stopped from ingesting. Once they ingest any pills, this becomes an attempt rather than an interrupted attempt. Shooting: Person has gun pointed toward self, gun is taken away by someone else, or is somehow prevented from pulling trigger. Once they pull the trigger, even if the gun fails to fire, it is an attempt. Jumping: Person is poised to jump, is grabbed and taken down from ledge. Hanging: Person has noose around neck but has not yet started to hang - is stopped from doing so.

1.66.field_description:
When person begins to take steps toward making a suicide attempt, but stops themselves before they actually have engaged in any self- destructive behavior. Examples are similar to interrupted attempts, except that the individual stops him/herself, instead of being stopped by
something else.

Acts or preparation towards imminently making a suicide attempt. This can include anything beyond a verbalization
or thought, such as assembling a specific method (e.g., buying pills, purchasing a gun) or preparing for one's death
by suicide (e.g., giving things away, writing a suicide note).
